newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS -Rate woes push gilt, short stg vols up.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS -Rate woes push gilt, short stg vols up.

text.p: Implied volatility of gilt and short sterling options edged higher on Thursday as the active market digested the full implications of Wednesday's British budget, brokers said.
Volatility was likely to remain strong with the threat to interest rate rises still hanging over the market, they said.

"Most of the news is out, but for short sterling obviously there are further rate hikes out there and you have still got a pretty volatile market," said Jonathan York, broker at Mees Pierson Derivatives in London.
Brokers quoted at-the-money implied volatility levels for short sterling at 9.10 percent middle for September versus 8.40 at Wednesday's close, and around 8.60 middle for December compared with 8.37.
At 1316 GMT, September short sterling futures were at 92.82, a fall of 0.16 on the day and suggesting interest rates at 7.10 percent by the end of the third quarter from 6.50 currently.
The December contract was at 92.60, down 22 basis points on the day suggesting interest rates of 7.40 percent by the end of the year.

British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown failed to relieve the perceived need for further rate hikes in his budget, shifting the focus to the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meeting next week.
Any decision on interest rates is expected on July 10.
Rate concerns also weighed on gilts. September gilt futures were at 114-08, down 17/32 on the day.
In options, brokers quoted implied volatility higher at 6.85 percent for September and 7.1 percent for December, compared with 6.80 and 6.90 percent respectively at Wednesday's close.
"Vol levels might drift off at the beginning of next week but they won't come off significantly, at least before the monetary policy committee meeting," said a European bank salesman in London.
"What is keeping things excited is that some people are for an eight percent base rate level by the end of the year," he added.
But traders said despite the budget disappointment, option vols were not as high as might be expected.
"Most of the flows are quiet bearish. People have been trading put ladders in the gilts and one-by-two call spreads in short sterling," said the salesman.
York said over the last couple of weeks there had been call buying and some combo trades.

"Most of the options trades were following a slightly bullish tack until you run into yesterday where, after a decent run up, they started to switch around and look for a little bit of protection, buying a few puts, selling a few call spreads," said the salesman.
